snippet.text: - Use as many branches as the work needs. A builder pushes each pull request to a branch of its own, named for its issue, such as `claude/issue-<n>-<words>`, and asks nobody before creating one: the maintainer said on 2026-11-20, in the coordinator's session, "they can use as many branches as they need", after builders in cloud sessions kept stopping to ask him for a second branch. That covers a builder's own branches for issues it has claimed. It never pushes to another builder's branch, to `main`, or to `melian/state`, and never forces a push.

message.text: The absolute ban on pushing another builder's branch assumes branch ownership never has to transfer, but the active issue-handoff decision explicitly allows a new builder to continue from a released builder's pushed branch, while the plan requires one issue to keep one pull request.

- A builder whose pull request has reached the merge queue, or whose lane has otherwise ended, takes the next such issue itself, without waiting to be assigned. If the queue then ejects its pull request, it comments `Released:` on the new issue and goes back. A cloud builder names its session for its state, and renames it at each change: `Active - issue #<n>` once it claims, `Active - issue #<n> - PR #<m>` once its draft is open, and `Passive - awaiting lane` only when it holds no issue or pull request to work on. A queue ejection sends it back to `Active - issue #<n> - PR #<m>` for the ejected pull request. It skips an issue whose brief needs what its session lacks, such as the host's store or live credentials, and leaves it for a session that has them. The claim rule below settles two builders choosing the same issue. [The decision](docs/decisions/2026-11-08-builders-take-the-next-issue.md) says why.

- One issue is one pull request. A step that needs several is split into an issue per pull request, each blocked by the one before. Open the draft with `Closes #<n>` in its description; a fix pass for a review finding works on the same issue and pull request.

## The rule

- A builder starts when its pull request is in the merge queue, not when it merges. If the queue then ejects that pull request, the builder comments `Released:` on the issue it took next and goes back to the ejected pull request. Another builder can then take the released issue, starting from any branch the first one pushed. A builder never holds a claim it isn't working on.
- It skips an issue its session cannot carry out, such as one that needs the host's Melian store, live model credentials, or a machine it is not on. A cloud session cannot run `melian compare` against the host's store, so a comparison record issue waits for the host.
- The claim rule decides between two builders that choose the same issue: the earliest writer's `Claim:` wins, and the other yields.
- The coordinator may still ask a session to take an issue. That session claims it as usual, and the claim rule still decides.

Choice: Each open step of a milestone, or each build part of a step, is a GitHub issue in that milestone, labelled `plan step`. The issue body is the builder's brief: the goal, the decisions to read, the scope, what done means, and the agent rules. GitHub's own relationships record the order: an issue is "blocked by" each issue it needs, and an agent never starts one with an open blocker. One issue is one pull request, so a step that spans several is split into an issue per pull request. A writer marks an issue `status: ready` when an agent may take it, and an agent trusts the brief only when a writer authored the issue and every edit of its body. An agent claims an issue as its first action: it swaps `status: ready` for `status: in progress`, comments `Claim:` with its name, where it runs (local, cloud VM or Codex) and its branch, and reads the comments again. The earliest claim since the issue was last marked ready wins; a later claimant comments that it yields and leaves the labels alone. A claim with no push for 24 hours is abandoned, and a writer releases it. The draft pull request says `Closes #N`, so the merge closes the issue. A builder works in a checkout of its own, which may be on another machine or a cloud VM, so a brief names nothing outside the repository and GitHub. There is no dispatcher. `docs/design-implementation-plan.md` keeps each step's design and reasons; the milestone's issues hold its status.

Why: The coordinator wrote every brief into a scratch file, so a brief was invisible to every agent but the one handed it, and it was gone when the session ended. Agents running in cloud VMs can't read the coordinator's scratch directory at all. An issue is readable by every agent wherever it runs, survives the session, and carries its dependencies in a form GitHub enforces. A dispatcher would be one more process that has to reach every machine. explanation.what: The absolute ban on pushing another builder's branch assumes branch ownership never has to transfer, but the active issue-handoff decision explicitly allows a new builder to continue from a released builder's pushed branch, while the plan requires one issue to keep one pull request.
explanation.whatToDo: Define a handoff exception: after a valid `Released:` and a new winning `Claim:`, transfer the existing issue branch/pull request to the new builder (or specify another mechanism that preserves the single pull request). Keep the ban for branches whose issue has not been handed off.
explanation.whyHere: A queue ejection can happen after the first builder has already pushed and opened the new issue's draft. The winning replacement builder cannot continue that existing pull request without updating its head branch; creating a fresh branch instead strands the draft or creates a second pull request for the issue.

properties.failureScenario: Builder A's earlier pull request enters the merge queue, so A claims issue 600, pushes `claude/issue-600-work`, and opens its required draft pull request. The earlier pull request is then ejected, so A releases issue 600 and returns to it. Builder B wins the next claim for issue 600. Under the new absolute rule B may not push A's branch, so B cannot update the existing draft; B must either abandon the already-pushed work or create a new branch and a second pull request, contrary to the active one-issue/one-pull-request decision and its released-work handoff.
